opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's a great question, and it's one we get a lot. The key difference is the granularity of the reconfigurability. An FPGA is reconfigurable at the bit level. You've got these lookup tables and a very fine-grained routing fabric, and you can build essentially any digital circuit you want out of them. That's tremendously flexible, but you pay for that flexibility. Most of the area and power on an FPGA goes into the interconnect and the configuration bits rather than into actual computation. So compared to an ASIC, you're typically looking at an order of magnitude or more in efficiency loss.

What we do with a reconfigurable dataflow architecture is raise the level of abstraction. Instead of bits, the basic units are coarse-grained: compute units that operate on vectors or tensors of words, with pipelined SIMD functional units, and memory units, which are distributed on-chip scratchpads with programmable address generation, plus a word-level, packet-switched interconnect connecting them. When you look at the applications we care about, machine learning and data analytics, they're built from a fairly small set of parallel patterns: map, reduce, zip, filter, and so on. So we said, let's build hardware that natively supports those patterns, and make reconfigurability operate at that level.

That gives you a couple of big advantages. First, efficiency. You're not spending most of your silicon on configurable routing of individual wires, so you get much closer to ASIC-level performance and energy efficiency while staying programmable. Second, and maybe more important, is programmability and compile time. With an FPGA you go through synthesis, place and route, timing closure, and that can take hours for a big design. And you're usually writing in something like Verilog, or at best high-level synthesis that still makes you think like a hardware designer. Because our fabric is coarse-grained and matches the structure of the computation, the compiler can take a dataflow graph straight from a framework like PyTorch or TensorFlow and map it onto the chip in minutes, not hours. That changes the whole developer experience.

The other piece is that we can reconfigure quickly at runtime. You can lay out a big chunk of a model spatially across the chip, stream data through it in a pipelined fashion, and keep intermediate results on chip instead of going back and forth to memory like a GPU does kernel by kernel. Then you can switch the configuration to the next part of the computation fast. So you get the spatial, pipelined execution benefit people like about FPGAs, but with the efficiency, the speed of compilation, and the software-friendliness you need to actually deploy it for large-scale ML.

So I'd summarize it this way: an FPGA is reconfigurable hardware for building circuits; a reconfigurable dataflow architecture is reconfigurable hardware for executing programs, specifically dataflow programs expressed in terms of parallel patterns.

fable-5.1.text:
Sure. So the fundamental difference is the granularity of reconfiguration. An FPGA is reconfigurable at the bit level. You've got lookup tables, you've got individual flip-flops, and you're wiring those together to build whatever you want, from a small state machine up to a full processor. That's incredibly flexible, but it comes at a cost. All of that bit-level routing and configuration overhead means you give up a lot of area and a lot of energy efficiency, and the compile times, the place-and-route times, can be hours.

What we do with the Reconfigurable Dataflow Unit is reconfigure at a much coarser grain. The building blocks are things like a pattern compute unit, which is essentially a SIMD pipeline of ALUs, and a pattern memory unit, which is a chunk of on-chip SRAM with address generation logic, and those are connected by a programmable interconnect. So instead of configuring individual gates, you're configuring how these fairly substantial compute and memory units are composed and how data flows between them. That matches the structure of machine learning workloads very well, because those workloads are really dense linear algebra and tensor operations with some parallel patterns around them. You don't need bit-level flexibility to express that.

The payoff is that you get most of the benefit of specialization, where the hardware looks like a custom circuit for the particular model you're running, without paying the FPGA tax. The compiler can map a dataflow graph onto the chip in minutes or seconds rather than hours, you keep the data on chip and streaming between units rather than bouncing through a memory hierarchy, and you can change that mapping as the model changes or as you move from one layer to the next. So I'd say an FPGA is reconfigurable hardware for arbitrary logic, and what we've built is reconfigurable hardware for dataflow, and that narrowing of the target is exactly what gives us the efficiency.

astra-6.text:
The main distinction is the granularity of the reconfiguration. An FPGA is configurable at the level of individual bits and logic functions. That gives you a tremendous amount of flexibility, but it also means there’s a lot of overhead in the configuration and routing needed to implement something like an arithmetic operation.

Our dataflow architecture is reconfigurable at a much coarser level. We have compute units that already perform arithmetic operations, along with memory units, and we configure how those units are connected and how data moves between them. So instead of building an adder out of configurable logic, we’re connecting existing arithmetic units to implement the computation.

You give up some of the FPGA’s ability to implement arbitrary digital logic, but you get much better efficiency for the workloads we’re targeting. And it gives the compiler a more direct way to map an application’s dataflow onto the hardware.

sol-6.1.text:
The key difference is the granularity of the reconfiguration. An FPGA is reconfigurable at the bit level. You have lookup tables and routing that let you construct essentially arbitrary digital logic. That’s very flexible, but there’s a substantial overhead in area, power, and performance.

Our dataflow architecture is reconfigurable at a much coarser level. We have units that already perform arithmetic operations, along with memory units, and we configure how those units operate and how data flows between them. So instead of building an adder out of programmable logic, you’re configuring an existing arithmetic unit and connecting it to other units.

That gives us the flexibility to map different computation graphs onto the hardware while getting much closer to the efficiency of specialized hardware. And the programming model is different: the compiler takes a high-level description of the computation and maps it spatially onto those compute and memory resources.
